aliases.name: Kaibyō
aliases.meaning: Generic term for supernatural cats including bakeneko and nekomata

aliases.name: Nabeshima no bakeneko
aliases.meaning: 'The Bakeneko of Nabeshima' — most famous Edo-period bakeneko story

description.summary: A class of yōkai in Japanese folklore: a domestic cat that has developed supernatural powers — shape-shifting, human speech, control of the dead — usually after living to a great age, growing very large, or possessing a long tail. Distinct from but closely related to the two-tailed nekomata.
description.full: Bakeneko (化け猫, 'changed cat' / 'monster cat') is a category of kaibyō (怪猫, supernatural cat) in Japanese folklore. According to widespread Edo-period belief, an ordinary cat might transform into a bakeneko on growing very old (commonly given as 7-13 years, with regional variation), reaching an unusual size, or developing a long tail. The bakeneko was credited with a wide repertoire of supernatural powers: shape-shifting into human form (often an elderly woman, sometimes the cat's own owner), walking upright on its hind legs, speaking human language, animating corpses, possessing humans, manipulating fire, and licking lamp-oil — a folk-belief that has plausible naturalistic roots in cats' attraction to fish-oil lamps. The most famous narrative is the Nabeshima no bakeneko sōdō ('Bakeneko Disturbance of Nabeshima'), set in 17th-century Saga (Hizen Province), in which a cat avenges its murdered mistress by tormenting the Nabeshima daimyō until killed by a loyal retainer. The story circulated in kōdan (oral storytelling), kabuki, and Edo kaidan-shū (collections of strange tales) including Mimibukuro and Kasshi Yawa. The bakeneko is closely related to the nekomata — the principal traditional distinction is that the nekomata has two tails while the bakeneko has only one. The bakeneko remains a recurring figure in modern Japanese popular culture, appearing in anime, manga, video games, and horror films.

etymology.origin: Japanese 化け (bake, from bakeru, 'to transform / become a ghost') + 猫 (neko, 'cat').
etymology.first_use: Established usage by the Edo period (1603-1868) in kaidan literature, kabuki, and ukiyo-e.

taxonomy.variant: Single-tailed bakeneko (vs. two-tailed nekomata); regional variants including the Saga / Nabeshima tradition

related_phenomena.name: Nekomata
related_phenomena.description: Two-tailed cat yōkai; closely related supernatural cat type.

related_phenomena.name: Kasha
related_phenomena.description: Cat-shaped yōkai that steals corpses from funerals.

related_phenomena.name: Maneki-neko
related_phenomena.description: Beckoning-cat figure of Japanese folk belief — non-malevolent companion to bakeneko/nekomata in popular culture.

related_phenomena.name: Kitsune
related_phenomena.description: Fox shapeshifter yōkai; a parallel domestic-animal supernatural figure.

related_phenomena.name: Tanuki
related_phenomena.description: Raccoon-dog shapeshifter; another long-lived animal yōkai.

features.description: Especially long-tailed cats are believed to be candidates for bakeneko transformation; in some regions owners docked kittens' tails to prevent it.
Reported to walk and dance on its hind legs.
In Edo iconography, bakeneko are often depicted dancing with a small cloth (tenugui) tied around the head.
Bakeneko are described as having grown unusually large before transforming.
A long-lived domestic cat (often given as 7-13 years) is the typical candidate for transformation.

physical.morphology: A domestic cat that, with age and other thresholds, develops yōkai attributes: bipedal posture, larger size, and human capabilities. In its most overt form may shape-shift entirely into human appearance.

abilities.description: Transforms into human form, most commonly an elderly woman; sometimes impersonates the cat's own deceased owner.
Reputed to leap over a corpse to animate it (a belief that supports the rite of guarding wakes against cats).
Possesses humans, often relatives of the cat's owner.
Reputed to manipulate or summon fire.
Drinks lamp-oil — a folk belief reflecting the use of fish-based oils in Edo lamps that cats genuinely found attractive.
Famously depicted dancing on hind legs at night, often with a cloth around the head.

habitat_preference: the homes of those who have wronged the cat
patterns: Transforms after long life with a human household
May avenge mistreatment of itself or its mistress
Otherwise mischievous rather than uniformly malevolent

range.description: Pan-Japanese folklore figure; locally inflected by regional traditions, with the most famous narrative cluster centred on Saga (former Hizen Province), home of the Nabeshima bakeneko tradition.

hotspots.name: Saga (Nabeshima domain)

location.description: Former Hizen Province, modern Saga Prefecture

hotspots.notes: Setting of the most famous bakeneko narrative.

first_recorded.source: Edo-period kaidan-shū (collections of strange tales) and kabuki playbills.

peak_activity_periods.description: Edo period — proliferation of bakeneko narratives in kaidan-shū, kabuki, ukiyo-e, and rakugo.
Toriyama Sekien-style yōkai compendia and the Mimibukuro / Kasshi Yawa traditions documenting bakeneko stories.

origins.cultural_roots: Japanese domestic culture: bakeneko folklore arose alongside the spread of cats as household animals from at least the Heian period and intensified in the Edo period when domestic cats were widespread.
origins.earliest_accounts: Edo-period kaidan-shū (e.g. Mimibukuro of Negishi Yasumori, c. 1782-1814) and kabuki performances anchor the figure in the 17th-19th centuries.
origins.folklore_connections: Closely tied to nekomata (two-tailed cat yōkai) and to a wider yōkai tradition of long-lived domestic animals (kitsune, tanuki) acquiring supernatural traits.

timeline.event: Bakeneko narratives proliferate in kaidan-shū, kabuki, rakugo, and ukiyo-e.
Negishi Yasumori compiles Mimibukuro (耳嚢), a kaidan-shū including bakeneko narratives.
Matsura Seizan compiles Kasshi Yawa (甲子夜話), a long miscellany including supernatural-cat anecdotes.
Kabuki adaptation 'Hana Sagano Nekomata Ishibumi' performed, contributing to the codification of the Saga bakeneko narrative on stage.
Mizuki Shigeru and modern yōkai-studies scholars synthesise the bakeneko tradition for popular audiences.
timeline.source: Mizuki Shigeru's yōkai compendia; Komatsu Kazuhiko's academic work.

history.modern_era: Bakeneko remain ubiquitous in modern Japanese popular culture, especially in anime, manga, video games, and horror cinema. They are stock characters in works by Mizuki Shigeru and have been the subject of academic reassessment by yōkai scholars (Komatsu Kazuhiko, Michael Dylan Foster).

documentary.name: Mimibukuro (耳嚢) — Negishi Yasumori
documentary.description: Edo-period miscellany of strange tales compiled by Negishi Yasumori; includes bakeneko anecdotes.

documentary.name: Saga / Nabeshima bakeneko kabuki tradition
documentary.description: Kabuki and kōdan performances dramatising the Nabeshima bakeneko sōdō; titles include 'Hana Sagano Nekomata Ishibumi' (1853).
documentary.source: Edo kabuki playbills and theatrical histories.

paranormal.name: Long-lived cats becoming yōkai
paranormal.description: The classic folk belief: a domestic cat that lives many years (7-13 by region) and develops a long tail or great size becomes a bakeneko, taking on shape-shifting and other supernatural powers.

skeptical.name: Naturalistic origins of cat folklore
skeptical.description: Several bakeneko traits have plausible naturalistic origins: cats' nocturnal eyes, static-electric fur, near-silent gait, retained predatory behaviour, and attraction to fish-based lamp-oils. Cumulative observation of these traits seeded supernatural attribution.

skeptical.name: Narrative-cultural construction
skeptical.description: The bakeneko, like other yōkai, is best understood as a culturally constructed figure consolidated through Edo-period kaidan literature, kabuki, and ukiyo-e rather than as a discrete creature.
evidence_cited: Studies of yōkai in Edo print culture; theatre history.

Kabuki and rakugo bakeneko performance tradition
stories: Nabeshima no bakeneko sōdō ('The Bakeneko Disturbance of Nabeshima', Saga, Edo period)
Various entries in Mimibukuro (Negishi Yasumori, c. 1782-1814)
Various entries in Kasshi Yawa (Matsura Seizan, 1821-1841)
folklore.beliefs: Domestic cats — especially long-tailed and long-lived ones — were widely treated with caution in Edo Japan. Wakes were guarded against cats believed capable of animating the dead, and tail-docking of kittens persisted in some regions to prevent transformation.

literature: Mizuki Shigeru, GeGeGe no Kitarō (1960-) and Yōkai Daizukai compendia
Lafcadio Hearn, In Ghostly Japan (1899) — touches on supernatural-cat motifs
Michael Dylan Foster, The Book of Yōkai (UC Press, 2015)
Hiroko Yoda and Matt Alt, Yokai Attack! (Tuttle, 2008/2012)
film_tv: Kuroneko (Kaneto Shindō, 1968) — black-cat ghost film with strong bakeneko / kaibyō motifs
Numerous tokusatsu and anime series featuring bakeneko characters
games: Shin Megami Tensei / Persona series — bakeneko / nekomata as recurring demons
Nioh series — bakeneko bosses and enemies
other: Recurring motif in ukiyo-e by artists including Utagawa Kuniyoshi (e.g. mid-19th-century cat prints) and Tsukioka Yoshitoshi
